newsitem.title: USA: Stocks power higher on late burst of buying.
newsitem.headline: Stocks power higher on late burst of buying.

text.p: Stocks rallied late Tuesday in a repeat of the previous day's performance, but the market had a cautious tone ahead of Wednesday's Congressional testimony by Federal Reserve Chairman Alan Greenspan.

The 30-stock Dow Jones industrial average ended up 29.63 points at 7,037.83, which was within flirting distance of its record close of 7,067.46 set one week ago. On Monday, the index soared 77 points.
In the broader market, advancing issues led declines 1,415 to 1,135 on active volume of 527 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
Investors again focused on a handful of big-name stocks, mostly to the exclusion of smaller issues.
"Money is continuing to go to large cap, quality names," said Guy Truicko, portfolio manager at Unity Management. "They have been and continue to be momentum plays."
International Business Machines Corp. was again among the strongest components of the Dow index, continuing its rebound from a recent broad technology sell-off. IBM rose 2-5/8 to 146-1/2.
Minnesota Mining and Manufacturing Co., another Dow component, rose 3-1/2 to 90.

The market's rally came despite an extremely cautious session in the bond market, which ground to a virtual stand-still ahead of Greenspan's semi-annual testimony to the Senate on Wednesday on the state of monetary policy and the economy.
Greenspan's second day of testimony to a House committee, was delayed to March 5 from the originally slated Feb. 27.
Even amid evidence that inflation currently poses little if any threat to the economy, analysts said the Fed chief's testimony, as always, will take centre stage.
In the bond market, the 30-year Treasury bond was unchanged and its yield was steady at Monday's close of 6.66 percent.
Recalling the market tumult that followed Greenspan's allusion to "irrational exuberance" during a speech two months ago, Truicko said, "I hope he doesn't decide to elaborate any further on that."
Even so, he noted, "We're up about 10 percent since those comments."

Investor caution ahead of the speech failed to dampen enthusiasm for blue chips, which continue to find buyers after every downturn and show little sign of pausing after their torrid run at the start the year.

"We continue to fracture the bears and frustrate the sideline money," said Alfred Goldman, chief market analyst at A.G. Edwards & Sons. "This market for six years now has bent but hasn't broken and that's how bull markets operate."
Technology stocks were generally higher, but the group remained sharply mixed in its performance.
Networking leader Cisco Systems Inc. dipped 2-1/2 to 56-1/2 after warning that declining capital spending and the strong dollar were eroding sales growth in some of its foreign markets.
Oil shares also were higher. Chevron Corp. gained 1-3/4 to 68 and Texaco Inc. rose 2-1/8 to 104-1/8.

The session's standout was recent castaway Centennial Technologies Inc., which rebounded sharply from its recent sell-off, surging 10-1/4 to 14-3/4 before the NYSE halted trading in the shares late in the day.

In an interview, Centennial's interim chief executive told Reuters the company posted record sales last week and said customers were not abandoning the company despite its recent disclosure of accounting irregularities that will force it to restate its results for this year and 1996.
ClinTrials Research Inc. skidded 13-3/4 to 9-1/2 after saying that it expected to post disappointing results for the latest quarter.
The Nasdaq Composite index rose 2.61 points to 1,347.69.
The Standard & Poor's composite index of 500 stocks rose 1.75 to 812.03. The American Stock Exchange index rose 1.92 to 599.99.
The NYSE Composite index of all listed common stocks rose 1.04 to 425.52. The average share was up 10 cents.
The Wilshire Associates Equity Index -- the market value of NYSE, American and Nasdaq issues -- was 7,747.559 up 20.159 or 0.26 percent.
